doctrine.statement: Joseph prospered in his work and in prison when Yahweh was with him. His master saw the results. Stephen recalls that God was with Joseph and delivered him from his afflictions. Caleb and Joshua appeal to Yahweh’s presence as grounds for courage. Jeremiah receives a promise of deliverance, and Haggai conveys Yahweh’s assurance to those rebuilding the house. In these passages his presence is shown in the help he gives his people.

Enoch walked with God, and Noah’s walk with God accompanies his righteousness and blamelessness. Malachi describes Levi’s walk in terms of true teaching, peace, uprightness and turning people from iniquity. Hebrews connects Enoch’s pleasing God with faith. Walking with God describes a life spent in his company through faith and upright conduct.

God establishes his covenant with Noah and his descendants. Yahweh makes a covenant with Abram concerning land for his descendants and names Isaac as the one with whom he will establish his everlasting covenant. Isaiah speaks of Yahweh’s covenant with Israel. Paul applies the covenant language to Israel when the deliverer comes and takes away their sins. These passages name the people and descendants with whom the covenant stands.

gloss: (object marker) the very one, untranslated; with suffixes me, him, them; (preposition) with, beside; (מֵאֵת) from
note: The object marker has the suffixed stem ʾōt-. Jewish Aramaic יַת with a third-person suffix can mean “he himself.” Hebrew’s reflexive uses and its marking of subjects fit an origin in a noun denoting the self. Phoenician ʾt before suffixes, Hebrew אוֹת “sign,” and Arabic إِيَّا and آيَة supply a possible connection through a person’s form or self. Al-Azhari offers the Arabic derivation with uncertainty, and a vocative origin has also been proposed. Hebrew אוֹת itself never means “self.” Aramaic אִיתַי “there is” corresponds to Hebrew יֵשׁ, with a different historical consonant, whereas the particle has t in Hebrew and Phoenician. Dan 3:12 uses both אִיתַי and יָתְהוֹן. The preposition has doubled t in ʾitt-. Phoenician ʾt and Akkadian itti share its uses, although older Akkadian išti complicates the sound correspondence and gives no support for deriving the preposition from ittu “sign.” OSHB lemmas 853 and 854 occur about 10,980 and 890 times respectively. Shared surface forms cause overlap in database counts. Later books sometimes spell the preposition אוֹת־ (2Ki 1:15, 3:12, Jer 12:1, 35:2, Isa 59:21, Ezk 2:6). Context distinguishes it there. אַתְּ “you” belongs with אַתָּה. The ploughshare אֵת, plural אִתִּים, is filed under אתת and is probably a loan (1Sa 13:20–21, Isa 2:4, Jol 4:10, Mic 4:3). Biblical Aramaic אָת “sign” belongs with אוֹת (Dan 3:32–33, 6:28). Possible name elements in אִתַּי and אִיתִיאֵל are treated separately. Greek normally expresses the object by the accusative. Ecclesiastes’ Greek σύν for the marker has no MACULA alignment here. Old Aramaic ʾyt at Sefire remains a lead. Ugaritic, which lacks an object marker, and Geʿez have not been examined further. The Akkadian comparison uses eBL.
summary: Two particles share the spelling אֵת. The commoner points out the definite thing a verb acts on, as in אֶת־הָאָרֶץ. With suffixes it gives אֹתִי “me” and אֹתָם “them.” It can also single out the subject of a sentence. The preposition, אִתִּי “with me” with a suffix, expresses company, Yahweh’s presence and help, dealings between parties, nearness and keeping. With מִן it means “from beside.” Syriac ܝܬ preserves both the nominal sense “being, self” and the object-marking use. Hebrew’s suffixed object marker can likewise mean “themselves” (Jer 7:19, Ezk 34:2). A derivation from אוֹת “sign” is uncertain. The preposition corresponds to Phoenician ʾt and Akkadian itti. No Hebrew verbal root is known for either particle.

senses.definition: Introduces the particular person or thing a verb acts on, ordinarily a definite noun identified by the article, a name or a possessive suffix.

Shem, Ham and Japheth each have the object marker.
The three sons each have their own object marker.
The stars form a further object of “made” alongside the two lights.
The livestock and the creeping things are the second and third of three individually marked objects.
Of the animals and birds that Yahweh God formed, the second phrase has the marker.

The text marks the harvest reaped and the sheaf brought.
אֶת־הָאָדָם marks the man whom God formed. The indefinite עָפָר follows without the particle.
אֵת יְהוָה introduces the one Israel is to love. Mat 22:37 expresses the object by the accusative.
The heavens and the earth each take אֵת as objects of “created.”

God made אֹתוֹ, the seventh day, holy.

Singular אֹתוֹ gives way to plural אֹתָם when male and female are named together.

“Do not leave us.”
Israel is to proclaim the appointed times as holy convocations.
The pronoun for the promised place is set before “I will give.”
The object of “bring out” can be expressed by the particle with a noun or with a suffix, including the full spelling אוֹתָם.
The suffixed particle identifies what Israel is to keep as a feast.
The adversary oppresses “you.”
The people God blessed are those he then addresses.
Noah is the one God had commanded.

senses.definition: Singles out the subject of a passive or intransitive verb, or the topic placed at the head of a sentence.

evidence.note: וְאֶת־הַבַּרְזֶל introduces the iron that fell into the water.

words.summary: About 11,000 occurrences, second in frequency to the conjunction. The unstressed form is אֶת־ under maqqef. With suffixes it takes the form אֹת־ or אוֹת־. Phoenician likewise distinguishes ʾyt and ʾt before a suffix. English generally leaves it untranslated, and Greek expresses the ordinary object by the accusative case. Its reflexive use and its occasional use with a subject single out the thing or person itself. Syriac ܝܬ preserves both the nominal and grammatical uses. The root behind the noun is uncertain.

senses.definition: The other party in something done between two: speech, covenant, kindness, or strife and war.

A covenant אֶת־מָוֶת, “with death,” stands parallel to an agreement וְעִם־שְׁאוֹל, “with Sheol.”

words.summary: About 900 occurrences. The suffixed forms include אִתִּי, אִתּוֹ and אִתָּנוּ. These distinguish the preposition from the object marker אֹתִי, אֹתוֹ. Some later texts write the preposition אוֹת־, so context decides the reading (2Ki 1:15, 3:12, Jer 12:1, Isa 59:21). It alternates with עִם in Jdg 7:4 and 2Sa 2:6. Phoenician ʾt and Akkadian itti share its uses, including a source with verbs of taking or receiving. Scripture supplies no verbal or nominal root for this preposition.

evidence.note: “He shall go with you” uses אִתָּךְ and “he shall not go with you” uses עִמָּךְ.
Kindness עִמָּכֶם is paired with doing good אִתְּכֶם.
The parallel concerning the spirit is in 1Sa 16:14.

After “come with us” in Num 10:29, Moses uses עִמָּנוּ of going with Israel.

evidence.note: דִּי־מַנִּיתָ יָתְהוֹן resumes the Jewish men in “whom you appointed,” literally “whom you appointed them.”

words.summary: Biblical Aramaic uses this form once, with a suffix, where Hebrew would have אֹתָם. Elsewhere Biblical Aramaic uses לְ to mark an object. The Targums use יַת as Hebrew uses אֵת. Syriac ܝܬ also denotes being or self.
